# Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic, Inc.

*Citation:* 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Addressed parallel California and Minnesota litigation over a non-compete; the Court held California courts should generally not enjoin a party from pursuing litigation in another state's courts, reversing a TRO — cautioning about interstate forum conflicts in non-compete disputes. Does not retreat from §16600's policy.

########## application_group_v_hunter.md
# Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.

*Citation:* 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's non-compete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; the Maryland choice-of-law clause did not control. California's policy against non-competes is 'fundamental'.

########## cal_bpc_16600.md
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. (b)(1) This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (2) This subdivision does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law.

########## cal_bpc_16600_1.md

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

########## cal_lab_925.md
# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. ########## restatement_187.md

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.

*Status in this library:* in force

*Citation:* 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Centel Cellular* (1994)** to the extent *Light* required the consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made. *Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

########## tx_jurisdiction_note.md

*Citation:* Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A forum-selection clause consenting to Travis County generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Wackenhut (Tex. 1990) applying Restatement §187 — the Texas Supreme Court refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy. Texas has a substantial relationship (place of contracting? employer's HQ — Meridian is Austin-based; Texas law chosen; place of performance is CA though). So §187(2)(a) probably satisfied — Texas has a substantial relationship. The fight is §187(2)(b): Is California's §16600 a "fundamental policy"? Yes — Application Group says California's policy against non-competes is "fundamental". Also Edwards + codification in §16600(b)(1) (read broadly, void "no matter how narrowly tailored"). Does California have a "materially greater interest" than Texas? Application Group holds California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's non-compete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; MD choice-of-law clause did not control. Here facts are analogous: out-of-state (Texas) employer, employee residing and working in California throughout. Note a wrinkle: in Application Group, the employee was recruited to work *for a California employer* (the competing California employer). Here Zhao worked for the Texas employer but remotely from California, and is joining a California competitor. Still, §16600.5(a)-(b) expressly reaches contracts "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" and prohibits attempting to enforce "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California" — that's the statutory answer to the Application Group wrinkle, i.e., California has asserted a materially greater interest.

Cal. Lab. Code §925(a): employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would (1) require adjudication outside CA of a claim arising in CA, or (2) deprive the employee of substantive protection of CA law for a controversy arising in CA. Here: no counsel involved — DocuSign 2 hours after receipt, no counsel requested or offered. §15 acknowledgment ("opportunity to consult counsel") does not satisfy §925(e), which requires actual individual representation in fact. §925(f): applies to contracts entered into on or after Jan 1, 2017 — this contract entered March 4, 2024, so it applies.

§15.50(a): enforceable if ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time made, to the extent limitations on time, geography, scope are reasonable and no greater restraint than necessary to protect goodwill/other business interest. §15.51(b): promisee bears burden where primary purpose is personal services. §15.51(c): reformation — court shall reform unreasonable limitations and enforce as reformed; no damages for breach before reformation. §15.52: exclusive remedies, preempts other criteria.

Sheshunoff (2006): covenant in at-will employment enforceable when employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential info) is performed, even if not at time of contracting; core inquiry is reasonableness under §15.50. # MEMORANDUM

**To:** General Counsel, Meridian Robotics, Inc.
**From:** Outside counsel
**Date:** October 25, 2026
**Re:** Enforceability of §8 (24-month nationwide non-compete) against Wei-Lin Zhao; whether to file in Travis County
**Privileged & confidential — attorney work product**

---

## 1. Question Presented

May Meridian enforce §8 of Zhao's employment agreement — a 24-month, nationwide bar on working for any business that designs or sells warehouse-logistics autonomous mobile robots — against a software engineer who resided and worked full-time in California, signed the form agreement by DocuSign two hours after receiving it without counsel, and is now employed in California by a competitor; and should Meridian file suit in Travis County, Texas, given that §14 chooses Texas law and a Travis County forum?

## 2. Brief Answer

**No on both counts. Do not file in Travis County, and do not send a demand letter threatening §8.**

- **Probability that California law governs the §8 question: ~85–90%.** Two independent routes get Zhao there: Cal. Lab. Code §925 (which, at his election, voids *both* halves of §14 and statutorily assigns California law and a California forum), and the Restatement §187 analysis that Texas and California courts both apply (under which California's §16600 policy is "fundamental" and California has the materially greater interest).
- **Probability Meridian obtains *any* §8 relief from any court: ~3% (range 1%–9%).**
- **Probability Meridian obtains relief that actually stops the Kestrel Autonomy job: ~1% (range 1%–3%).** Even a Texas injunction would face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds (`library/tx_jurisdiction_note.md`), so the realistic product of suit is an unenforceable order and two forums' worth of fees.
- **Probability Meridian §8 is held void/unenforceable as to Zhao if litigated: ~90% or better.** Under California law §8 is void on its face — §16600 as amended voids it "no matter how narrowly tailored," and the escape hatches (narrow-restraint, rule-of-reason) are foreclosed by *Edwards* and *Ixchel*.
- **Probability Meridian creates affirmative liability for itself by filing: ~85–90%, essentially one-way.** §16600.5 makes the *attempt to enforce* a void contract a civil violation, and makes a fee award to a prevailing employee mandatory. Meridian's exposure starts the moment it files — before it can lose.
- **Expected net cost of filing: roughly −$600k** (range −$390k to −$900k, before any company-wide notice/UCL claims). Arithmetic in §7.

The bad news stated plainly: §8 is not merely hard to enforce against this employee — **meridian's own conduct has already generated liability independent of the lawsuit.** Meridian (i) put a clause in a California employee's contract that California makes unlawful to include, and (ii) skipped a statutory notice obligation company-wide (ticket LO-233). Zhao's departure is now mostly a compliance-and-remediation problem, not a litigation problem.

---

## 3. Facts

From `documents/employment_agreement_excerpt.pdf`, `documents/hr_timeline.md`, `documents/resignation_email.txt`.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2024-02-28 | Offer letter emailed by Austin HR to the candidate **in Oakland, CA**; states "**fully remote from California**." |
| 2024-02-14 | *(Company-wide)* AB 1076 notice deadline; legal's notice project "**deprioritized**" per legal-ops ticket **LO-233**; **no notice sent to California employees**. |
| 2024-03-04 | Agreement sent 9:12 a.m.; **signed via DocuSign 11:05 a.m.** (≈2 hours). No negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered; **standard form for all engineers**. |
| 2024-03-04 → 2026-09-30 | Worked from Oakland. **Two** trips to Austin HQ (onboarding, Mar. 2024; offsite, Oct. 2025). |
| 2026-09-16 | Resignation email: joining **Kestrel Autonomy, Fremont, CA**; has consulted a **California employment attorney**; states he will honor confidentiality and take nothing. |
| 2026-09-30 | Termination effective. §8's 24-month clock would run to **2028-09-30**. |
| 2026-10-13 | Kestrel start date (**assumed to have occurred — see Open Items**). |
| 2026-10-02 | GC question. **Today is 2026-10-25 — 25 days post-termination, ~12 days post-start.** |

**Key contract terms.** §8: 24 months, "anywhere in the United States," any business "engaged in the design or sale of autonomous mobile robots for warehouse logistics." §9: 12-month employee/customer non-solicitation. §10: standard confidentiality/inventions. §14: Texas law; exclusive jurisdiction and venue in Travis County. §15: "Employee acknowledges having had the opportunity to consult counsel" — contradicted by Meridian's own HR file note in the same exhibit ("Employee signed via DocuSign 2 hours after receipt; **no counsel involved**").

**Facts Meridian created for Zhao.** The offer letter's "fully remote from California" line is Meridian's own proof that Zhao "primarily resides and works in California" (§925(a)). The two-hour DocuSign turnaround, "standard form for all engineers," and "no negotiation" are Meridian's own proof that the clauses were **required as a condition of employment** (§925(a)) and were not individually negotiated (§925(e)). The §15 recital does not help and hurts: it is contradicted by the HR file in the same document set, which reads as papering over the §925(e) exception.

---

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Which law applies, and why

**Both states use the same test, so the clause is analyzed identically whichever court sits.** Texas applied Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187 in *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990) (`library/desantis_v_wackenhut.md`); California follows §187 in *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992) (`library/nedlloyd_v_superior_court.md`). Under §187(2) the chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties/transaction, **or** (b) application of the chosen law would be contrary to a **fundamental policy** of a state with a **materially greater interest** that would supply the law absent the clause (`library/restatement_187.md`).

- **Prong (a) probably does not help Zhao.** Texas has a substantial relationship: Meridian's HQ, the offer issued by Austin HR, the chosen law, the chosen forum. Assume this prong fails.
- **Prong (b) is where Meridian loses.** California's policy against employee non-competes is expressly "fundamental" (`library/application_group_v_hunter.md`), and it has been codified and *hardened* since 1998: §16600(b)(1) now directs broad reading in line with *Edwards* and voids non-competes "no matter how narrowly tailored" (`library/cal_bpc_16600.md`), while §16600.5(a)–(b) makes the voidness apply "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" and forbids attempts to enforce "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California" (`library/cal_bpc_16600_5.md`). Those two clauses are the California Legislature's own assertion of a materially greater interest, aimed at exactly Meridian's fact pattern.
- **The mirror image of *DeSantis* is the problem.** In *DeSantis* the Texas Supreme Court **refused to honor a Florida choice-of-law clause** in a non-compete because the state where the employee worked (Texas) had the materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy. A California court applying *Nedlloyd* + *Application Group* will run that same machine in reverse and land on §16600. A Texas court applying *DeSantis* is being asked to distinguish its own precedent — it can do so (Zhao worked in California, not Texas; in *Application Group* the employee had been recruited to work **for a California employer**), but it must first explain why the materially-greater-interest state is Texas when the employee lived, worked, and will compete in California for the entire two years.
- **§188 contacts are split, but the center of gravity is California:** residence and place of performance (24 of 24 months) = CA; place of contracting = mixed (offer issued from Austin; executed electronically in CA); employer domicile = TX; locus of the alleged competitive injury = CA; the restraint's entire geographic target includes CA.
- **The decisive point is that §187 is not the only route.** Cal. Lab. Code §925(b) makes §14 **voidable by Zhao**, and once voided at his request, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and **California law shall govern the dispute**" (`library/cal_lab_925.md`). That is a statutory assignment of law and forum that does not depend on winning the §187 argument. See §4.3.

**Conclusion:** California law governs the §8 question in ~85–90% of realistic outcomes. Any litigation plan should be built on that assumption, not on the choice-of-law clause.

### 4.2 Enforceability under each law

**Under California law (most likely applicable): §8 is void.**

- §16600(a) voids every contract restraining "a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind," and (b)(1) requires it be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards*," voiding any employment non-compete "no matter how narrowly tailored" that does not satisfy a statutory exception (`library/cal_bpc_16600.md`).
- *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008) (`library/edwards_v_arthur_andersen.md`) forecloses the intuitive argument that a field-specific carve-out is a "narrow restraint": "Noncompetition agreements are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions." *Edwards* expressly disapproved *Campbell v. Board of Trustees*, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987) and *General Commercial Packaging*, 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997) — both of which are in this library flagged **superseded** and must not be argued (`library/campbell_v_stanford_1987.md`, `library/general_commercial_packaging_1997.md`).
- *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020) closes the other door: the rule of reason applies to **business-to-business** restraints; the employment context is governed by *Edwards* and non-competes are void (`library/ixchel_v_biogen.md`). §8 is squarely an employment restraint.
- **Residual uncertainty, flagged:** §16600 voids restraints "[e]xcept as provided in this chapter," and the chapter's exceptions (sale of business/dissolution-type carve-outs) are **not in this library**. Nothing in our facts suggests one applies (Zhao sold no interest), so this is a formality, not a route. I also cannot state with library support whether §9 (12-month non-solicit) is void; *Edwards*'s library summary addresses non-competition agreements, and §16600(b)(1) speaks to noncompete clauses. Treat §9 as at material risk but unresolved, and note that if it functions as a de facto restraint on taking the Kestrel role it invites the same §16600.5 exposure.

**Under Texas law (the fallback Meridian is hoping for): §8 clears the threshold and then probably fails on scope — and the statutory remedy is reformation with no pre-reformation damages.**

- **Ancillary element — probably satisfied.** §§15.50(a) requires the covenant be "ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made" (`library/tex_bcc_15_50.md`). *Light v. Centel Cellular*, 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994) set the two-part test but its **timing** requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (`library/light_v_centel_1994.md`, status: **modified** — and the library expressly warns it "should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant"). *Sheshunoff Management Services v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006) holds the covenant is enforceable where the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at contracting, and redirects the "core inquiry" to §15.50 reasonableness (`library/sheshunoff_v_johnson.md`). *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011) rejected a narrow "give rise" requirement and accepted consideration reasonably related to protecting goodwill (`library/marsh_usa_v_cook.md`). So §10's confidentiality/invention promises, performed, likely get §8 past the ancillary gate. **This is Meridian's best Texas point and it only gets to the second question.**
- **Reasonableness — the likely failure.** §15.50(a) requires limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** that are reasonable and impose "no greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the promisee's goodwill. §8 is 24 months × the entire United States × the entire field of warehouse-logistics AMRs, for one perception engineer, with no carve-out for non-competing work. Under §15.51(b), **Meridian bears the burden** because the agreement's primary purpose is personal services. A restraint covering an entire industry nationwide, entered on a form with no negotiated confidentiality-specific consideration tied to Zhao, is on its face broader than "necessary."
  - *Flagged as unverified:* **this library contains no Texas case assessing a 24-month, nationwide, industry-wide restraint.** My conclusion that the scope is unreasonable is an inference from the text of §15.50(a), not a cited holding. Do not let it be presented in a brief as case-supported on this library.
- **Remedy ceiling even if Meridian wins:** §15.51(c) — the court **shall reform** an over-broad covenant and enforce it as reformed, **but may not award damages for breach before reformation**. So the Oct. 13 start at Kestrel generates **no damages** in the branch where Meridian "wins" by reformation. §15.52 makes §§15.50–15.51 procedures and remedies **exclusive and preemptive** of other criteria, which also forecloses laundering the claim as a common-law restraint-of-trade or choice-of-law-breach theory.
- §8's clock: termination 2026-09-30 → 24 months runs to **2028-09-30**; a reformed 12-month covenant would end **2027-09-30**, and 25 days (≈3.4% of the period) have already run. Texas courts cannot give the time back.

### 4.3 Cal. Lab. Code §925 — the clause that ends the plan

Every element is satisfied on Meridian's own documents (`library/cal_lab_925.md`):

| §925 element | Fact | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Employer "require[s]" the provision **as a condition of employment** | Standard form for all engineers; sent 9:12 a.m., signed 11:05 a.m.; "no negotiation" | Met |
| Employee "**primarily resides and works in California**" | Offer states "fully remote from California"; two years of Oakland work; two short trips | Met |
| Provision requires adjudication **outside California** of a claim arising in California | §14 exclusive Travis County forum | Met |
| Provision **deprives** the employee of California's substantive protection | §14 chooses Texas law over §16600 | Met |
| §925(f): contract entered/modified/extended **on or after 1/1/2017** | Executed 2024-03-04 | Applies |
| §925(e) exception: employee "**in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating" the venue/choice-of-law terms | HR file: "no counsel involved"; nothing requested or offered | **Exception unavailable.** §15's recital of an "opportunity" to consult counsel is not actual representation, and is contradicted by Meridian's own HR note in the same exhibit. Representation retained in 2026 does not retroactively satisfy a formation-date test. |

**Consequences.** §925(b): the offending provisions are **voidable by the employee**, and if voided at his request "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern." §925(c): a court **may** award Zhao fees for enforcing §925 rights. Zhao has already stated, through counsel, that he will void both the forum and choice-of-law clauses.

**Knock-on effect on jurisdiction.** Our own practice note is candid: the forum clause "generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; **but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925** at the employee's election, the Texas court must find **independent minimum contacts**," and "two short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer **may or may not suffice**" (`library/tx_jurisdiction_note.md`, citing Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042 and *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)). So losing §925 does not just move the case — it may mean Meridian cannot even hale Zhao into Travis County.

**The one real defense here, and its limits:** §925's text is not expressly limited to California-domiciled employers, and this library contains **no authority** on whether §925 reaches a Texas employer of a California-resident remote employee. That is a genuine open question and I cannot verify it in the library. Relatedly, the firm's 2024 memo relies on *Westbrook Systems v. Ng* for the proposition that §16600.5 lacks extraterritorial reach over out-of-state employers — but (i) that case is **not in this library**, (ii) the firm's own 2025 memo records that the Ninth Circuit **granted rehearing en banc** (argued Jan. 2025) with **no disposition in our file**, and (iii) §16600.5(b) is drafted to negate exactly that argument ("regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California"). Treat the extraterritoriality defense as a lottery ticket, not a plan.

### 4.4 §16600.5 exposure — suing creates the liability

`library/cal_bpc_16600_5.md`:

- **(c)** "An employer shall **not enter into** a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter." Meridian did that in March 2024 — **already complete, before any lawsuit.**
- **(b)** An employer "shall **not attempt to enforce**" a void contract, regardless of where signed or where employment was maintained. Filing in Travis County *is* the attempt. So is a demand letter that threatens §8 (reading; the library does not define "attempt").
- **(d)** Entering into **or** attempting to enforce a void contract "commits a **civil violation**."
- **(e)(1)** Zhao may bring a **private action** for injunctive relief and/or actual damages. **(e)(2)** a prevailing employee "**shall** be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs" — **mandatory**, not discretionary.

Two features make this asymmetric. First, **the clock runs against Meridian from the filing date**: it cannot settle out of the exposure by declining to win; declining to *file* is the only thing that caps it. Second, **continuing** to prosecute after §925 voids §14 is itself an ongoing "attempt to enforce."

**Company-wide.** §8 is the **standard form for all engineers**. Every California-resident engineer hired on that form since §16600.5 took effect on 1/1/2024 has the same (c) claim, and — if they were current employees on 2024-02-14 — the same notice claim. Zhao is one instance of a program defect, and a public lawsuit is the most likely way the rest of the population learns about it. **Quantifying this requires headcount data we do not have** (Open Item 1).

*Flagged:* whether Zhao's §16600.5(e)(1) "actual damages" are anything beyond nominal for an employee who simply kept working are unknowable here; the **fee award**, not damages, is the driver. Also flagged: the library does not contain the text of Bus. & Prof. Code §17200 or its remedies, so I cannot opine on UCL remedies beyond §16600.1(c)'s incorporation (below).

### 4.5 AB 1076 / §16600.1 notice — a real problem, with one genuine wrinkle

`library/cal_bpc_16600_1.md`:

- **(a)** "It shall be **unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract**, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception." Subdivision (a) has **no date qualifier**. Zhao's contract includes §8. That is a violation on the face of the statute, and (c) makes it "an act of unfair competition within the meaning of" §17200. This limb is **not** cured by notice and does **not** depend on the notice project.
- **(b)(1)** The **notice** duty runs to "**current employees**" and "former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022," and was due "**by February 14, 2024**," in individualized writing to last known mailing **and** email addresses.
- **The wrinkle — and it is narrower than it looks.** Zhao was **not** an employee on 2024-02-14: the offer is dated 2024-02-28 and the agreement took effect 2024-03-04. He was therefore neither a "current employee" on the deadline date nor a "former employee employed after January 1, 2022" at that time. On the text in this library, the **February 14, 2024 notice obligation arguably never attached to Zhao**, and the library contains **no authority** resolving whether §16600.1(b) creates an ongoing notice duty for employees hired *after* the deadline. That is the *only* place Meridian has a defense in this whole file, and it is narrow:
  1. It defends **only** the (b) notice limb — not (a), and not §16600.5.
  2. It **cuts against** Meridian elsewhere: for any California engineer who *was* a current employee on 2024-02-14 and had §8 in their contract, the LO-233 "deprioritized" decision is a clean, documented (b) violation → (c) unfair competition. **Meridian's exposure is to that population, not to Zhao.**
- **The documents are the problem.** LO-233 records that legal identified the obligation and the company chose to deprioritize it. In a fee-and-unclean-hands narrative, that is the worst kind of exhibit. Two immediate operational consequences: (i) **litigation-hold LO-233 and the notice project now** — do not let anyone "clean up" the ticket; (ii) do not let the deprioritization decision travel into a filing.

**Remediation judgment call (needs your decision, not mine):** sending §16600.1(b)-style notices now to current and qualifying former California employees is cheap, is the conduct the statute asks for, and mitigates; but it also memorializes that §8 is void in California and hands California-resident engineers a roadmap. My recommendation in §6 is to send them, and to stop using §8 for California-resident hires immediately — the (a) limb keeps accruing with every new California hire on the form.

### 4.6 Remedies and fee exposure

**What Meridian can realistically get, even in its best branch.**

| Branch | Probability | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| §925 election succeeds → CA forum, CA law | ~0.85 × 0.95 ≈ **81%** | §8 void; no relief; Zhao's §16600.5 claims live |
| §925 fails → Travis County, TX law | ~0.15 × 0.90 × 0.50 ≈ **7%** | Ancillary gate cleared (*Sheshunoff*/*Marsh*); likely **reformation** under §15.51(c); **no damages pre-reformation**; any order unenforceable in CA |
| §925 fails → Travis County, CA law | ~7% | §8 void |
| §925 fails → no independent minimum contacts | ~1.5% | No jurisdiction; dismissal |

- **Injunction:** requires an independently enforceable covenant plus irreparable harm. Zhao has affirmatively stated he will honor confidentiality and take nothing; there is **no trade-secret misappropriation allegation in this file**. (Note: trade-secret law is **not in this library** — no UTSA/DTSA — so any such claim must be researched before anyone drafts it; I express no view.)
- **Damages:** barred before reformation by §15.51(c). Zhao's actual competitive harm to Meridian is speculative.
- **Fees:** the agreement excerpt contains **no prevailing-party fee clause**, so Meridian has no contractual fee route. §15.52 makes §§15.50–15.51 remedies exclusive. Zhao, by contrast, has **two** statutory fee bases: §16600.5(e)(2) (mandatory) and §925(c) (discretionary). The fee-shifting is strictly one-directional.
- **Delay already incurred:** 25 days have passed since termination and ~12 days since the Kestrel start. Emergency relief depends on showing immediate, irreparable injury; a plaintiff who waits through the start date invites the response that the harm is neither imminent nor irreparable. (General practice point; no library authority speaks to it.)
- **Personal jurisdiction:** only if §14 survives; otherwise Meridian must prove minimum contacts on two short trips (`library/tx_jurisdiction_note.md`).
- **Parallel-litigation reality:** *Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic*, 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002) says California courts should **generally not enjoin a party from litigating in another state's courts** (`library/advanced_bionics_v_medtronic.md`). To be fair to the pro-filing view: this means Zhao probably cannot simply enjoin Meridian out of Travis County, so a Texas case can be kept alive. But *Advanced Bionics* "does not retreat from §16600's policy," and a Texas injunction "would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds" (`library/tx_jurisdiction_note.md`). The realistic product is not leverage — it is **Meridian funding two courts to litigate the same clause to the same result.**

**No federal shield.** The FTC Non-Compete Rule is **vacated** — set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024); the FTC dismissed its appeal in September 2025; it never took effect (`library/ftc_noncompete_rule_16cfr910.md`, status **vacated**; `library/ryan_llc_v_ftc.md`, in force). It cannot be cited for anything except the fact that it is gone. **Correction to the file:** the 2025 firm memo says "the FTC rule [was] **enjoined**." That is wrong and it matters — vacatur under the APA erases the rule; an injunction binds only the parties. Whoever relied on "enjoined" in another matter should be corrected. (The 2025 memo's bottom line — state law controls — is right.)

---

## 5. The strongest argument for each side

**Meridian's best case.** (1) §187(2)(a) is satisfied and prong (b) is not: this is not *Application Group*, where the employee had been recruited to work **for a California employer in California**; Zhao contracted with a Texas employer whose goodwill, HQ, and competitive stake sit in Austin, and §188's place of contracting points to Texas. *DeSantis* protects the policy of the state with the greater interest — and a Texas court is entitled to ask whether California's interest is materially greater than Texas's merely because the employee chose where to live. (2) *Application Group* predates SB 699, and §16600.5's extraterritorial reach is contested (*Westbrook*, per the firm's own file, under en banc review) — so the statute doing the work is not settled law. (3) On the merits, *Sheshunoff* and *Marsh USA* clear the ancillary gate, §15.51(c) makes **reformation** the statutory answer rather than invalidation, and no Texas statute caps 24 months or nationwide geography. (4) §15 recites an opportunity to consult counsel. (5) *Advanced Bionics* means California should not enjoin the Texas suit.

*Why it still loses:* points 1 and 2 are unverifiable in this library; point 3 gets to the merits only to reach a reasonableness problem under §15.50(a) on a burden Meridian carries (§15.51(b)), with damages foreclosed pre-reformation; point 4 is contradicted by Meridian's own HR note, so it evidences the §925(e) problem instead of curing it; and point 5 buys forum, not outcome.

**Zhao's best case.** (1) §925(a)–(b) is a statutory kill shot on §14 built out of Meridian's own documents — offer letter ("fully remote from California"), HR file ("standard form," "no negotiation," "no counsel involved"), executed 2024 — and §925(e) is unavailable because he was not **in fact** individually represented in negotiating §14. Void §14 and California law and a California forum follow by statute, with a discretionary fee award under §925(c). (2) §16600(a) + (b)(1) + *Edwards* void §8 "no matter how narrowly tailored"; *Ixchel* bars the rule-of-reason recharacterization; *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* are dead. (3) §16600.5(a)–(b) removes "you signed it in Texas / employment was in Texas" from the argument. (4) §16600.5(b)+(d) convert Meridian's own lawsuit into a civil violation with **mandatory** fees. (5) §16600.1(a) makes including §8 unlawful *per se*, actionable as unfair competition.

---

## 6. Recommendation

1. **Do not file in Travis County. Do not assert §8.** Probability of meaningful relief ≈ 1–3%; probability of creating §1660.5 liability by filing ≈ 85–90%; expected net cost ≈ −$600k. Even the "deterrence" rationale is thin: a case this likely to be dismissed on jurisdiction and choice of law does not deter other engineers; a fee award against Meridian that other engineers' counsel read about does the opposite.
2. **Do not send a §8 demand or cease letter.** Under §16600.5(b), the threat is the violation. If a letter has already gone out, tell me today — it changes the exposure analysis (Open Item 2).
3. **Protect what is actually protectable.** Enforce §10: written recall/certification-of-deletion demand for Meridian data and devices, device-return audit, revoke access, and — if you have evidence of actual data taken — that is a trade-secrets conversation. Note the library contains **no trade-secret authority**, so that claim requires separate research before filing.
4. **Do not build a case around §9 either.** Its California status is unresolved on this library, and asserting it as a stand-in for §8 re-creates the same §16600.5 exposure.
5. **Fix the form now.** Stop using §8 (and §9 as written) for California-resident hires immediately. Every California hire on the current form is a fresh §16600.5(c) violation. Substitute confidentiality, invention-assignment, non-solicit where lawfully usable, and — for future Texas-based hires only — a genuinely ancillary, role-tailored covenant negotiated with real consideration. (Paid notice-period/"garden leave" structures are **not** covered by this library; flag if you want that analyzed.)
6. **Send the §16600.1-style notices** to current California employees and qualifying former employees (employed after 1/1/2022) whose contracts contain §8, by individualized writing to last known mailing **and** email address; document it; and close LO-233 with a compliance record. On Zhao specifically the duty arguably never attached (he was hired after 2/14/2024), but voluntary notice to the population that *was* covered is the cheapest mitigation available, and the (b) exposure lives with that population.
7. **Litigation-hold and preserve**: LO-233 and the notice project, the DocuSign metadata (9:12 a.m./11:05 a.m. is already in your own file), the "standard form for all engineers" template history, and the §15 recital's drafting history. Nothing gets deleted.
8. **Quantify the population.** Report: number of California-resident engineers on the §8 form, by hire date relative to 2024-02-14 and 2024-01-01, and whether any §8 has been asserted or a notice sent for them. Exposure per §7 is roughly linear in that headcount.
9. **Audit the two internal memos.** They are background, not authority; the authorities inside them (*Calderon*; *Westbrook*) are **not in this library** and *Westbrook* was, as of the last entry in the file, under **en banc rehearing with no recorded disposition**. The 2024 memo's recommendation of suit "in the Alvarez matter" rests on those cases — please confirm Alvarez's status, because if Meridian sued there, the §16600.5 analysis above may already be live on an existing docket.
10. **Rebuild the memo bank**: correct "enjoined" → "vacated/set aside nationwide, never took effect"; obtain the *Westbrook* en banc disposition; label *Calderon* and *Westbrook* unverified until pulled and Shepardized by someone with a subscription.

**If you decide to file anyway** (I advise against it): file, do not serve a demand letter first; brief §925 and personal jurisdiction up front rather than assuming §14 carries the day; plead §10 confidentiality claims as the primary theory and §8 as a reformation claim under §15.51(c); budget ~$250–500k; and expect a California cross-action within weeks.

---

## 7. The arithmetic

Inputs are **stated estimates**, not library facts, and are labelled as such. Money inputs are illustrative planning figures with no support in this library; correct them with your budget data.

**7.1 Probability tree**

```
P(925 election fails)                    = 1 - 0.85              = 0.15
P(Travis Cty personal jurisdiction | so) = 0.90  (forum clause stands)
   branch to Travis County               = 0.15 x 0.90           = 0.135
P(Texas law applied by TX court)         = 0.50
   relief if TX law  = 0.15 (reasonable as written) + 0.30 (usefully reformed) = 0.45
   relief if CA law  = 0.05
   inner expectation = 0.50 x 0.45 + 0.50 x 0.05                = 0.250

P(any §8 relief)          = 0.135 x 0.250                       = 0.0338 -> 3.4%
P(relief that stops the job) = 0.0338 x 0.35 (CA non-recognition) = 0.0118 -> 1.2%
P(California law governs §8) = 0.85 x 0.95 + 0.135 x 0.50 + 0.015  = 0.89 -> 89%
```

Sensitivity (rows = P(Zhao wins §925); columns = P(Texas court keeps Texas law)):

| q1 \ pTX | 0.30 | 0.50 | 0.70 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.70 | 4.6% | 6.8% | 8.9% |
| 0.80 | 3.1% | 4.5% | 5.9% |
| **0.85** | 2.3% | **3.4%** | 4.5% |
| 0.90 | 1.5% | 2.2% | 3.0% |
| 0.95 | 0.8% | 1.1% | 1.5% |

Even the most Meridian-friendly cell in the grid (70% chance Zhao loses §925 *and* 70% chance Texas law survives *and* the court reforms a nationwide 24-month covenant) is **under 9%**. **Range carried into the Brief Answer: 1%–9% for any relief; 1%–3% for relief that actually works.**

**7.2 Exposure if Meridian files**

```
P(§16600.5(c) violation: entered contract with void clause) = 0.85
P(§16600.5(b) violation: attempted to enforce)              = 0.80
P(at least one) = 1 - (1-0.85)(1-0.80)                      = 0.970
P(Zhao asserts counterclaims)                              = 0.90
P(faces affirmative CA liability) = 0.970 x 0.90            = 0.87  -> ~85-90%
```

**7.3 Cost/benefit of filing (all $ figures are assumptions)**

```
Benefit   = 150k (midpoint settlement/deterrence value) x 0.034 =    +5.1k
Own fees  = midpoint of 250k-500k (TX suit + CA counter-action) =  -375k
Adverse   = midpoint of 150k-400k x 0.85 (fee award probability)=  -234k
                                                               ----------
EV(filing)                                                   =  -603.6k
Best case  = 250 x 0.034 - 250 - 150 = -391.5k
Worst case =  50 x 0.034 - 500 - 400 = -898.3k
```

Filing is not close to breaking even on any plausible input; the benefit term is an order of magnitude smaller than either fee term, and §16600.5(e)(2)'s fee award is **mandatory** once Zhao prevails.

**7.4 Pattern exposure (headcount unknown — Open Item 1)**

Per California-resident engineer on the §8 form, assume $20k–$60k resolution value (§16600.5 claims are fee-driven, so this is crude):

| N engineers | at $20k | at $60k |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | $100k | $300k |
| 12 | $240k | $720k |
| 25 | $500k | $1,500k |

**7.5 Dates**

```
§8 period if enforced as written : 2026-09-30 + 24 months = 2028-09-30
§8 if reformed to 12 months      : 2026-09-30 + 12 months = 2027-09-30
Days elapsed as of 2026-10-25     : 25 days = 3.4% of the 24-month period
```

**Not reconciled, deliberately:** I have not forced 7.4 into 7.3, because 7.4 depends on headcount we do not have and on whether a public filing triggers the other employees' claims at all. Both numbers are left open.

---

## 8. Assumptions, and what I could not verify

**Assumptions stated prominently (also in `QUESTIONS.md`):**
1. Zhao began work at Kestrel Autonomy on or about 2026-10-13, and Kestrel designs/sells warehouse-logistics AMRs (so §8 is facially implicated).
2. Meridian is a Delaware/Texas-headquartered corporation with HQ in Travis County; no demand or cease letter has yet been sent to Zhao.
3. The agreement excerpt is complete as to fee-shifting — there is **no** prevailing-party attorney-fee clause anywhere in the full agreement.
4. Zhao was never a California employee of Meridian before 2024-02-14 (first engagement 2024-02-28/2024-03-04), and had no prior Meridian contract that §8 was added to by amendment (which would raise §925(f) "modified or extended" and §16600.1(b) "current employee" questions differently).
5. No confidential information is missing; the file contains no trade-secret-misappropriation evidence.

**Things I believe but could NOT verify in this library — labelled, not cited:** the §16600 statutory exceptions; the text and remedies of Bus. & Prof. Code §17200; any Texas case on the reasonableness of a 24-month nationwide industry-wide covenant; whether §925 or §16600.5 apply to an out-of-state employer of a California-resident remote employee; whether "attempt to enforce" includes a pre-suit demand; whether §16600.5(e)'s private action reaches a §16600.1(a) violation ("this chapter"); the California status of customer/employee non-solicitation clauses; trade-secret law; standards for TRO/TPI, anti-suit injunctions, or forum non conveniens; all limitations periods; and *Calderon* and *Westbrook* (not in the library at all).

**Authority-status audit of what I relied on:** *Campbell* (superseded by *Edwards*), *General Commercial Packaging* (superseded by *Edwards*), and the FTC Rule (vacated, *Ryan*) are discussed **only** for the proposition that they are no longer available; *Light v. Centel* (modified by *Sheshunoff*) is discussed only for its ancillary test with the timing holding disclaimed. Every other authority relied on is marked in force in `library/INDEX.md`. Full mapping in `citations.json`.

{"path": "/work/workspace/deliverable/memo.md", "content": "# MEMORANDUM

**To:** General Counsel, Meridian Robotics, Inc.
**From:** Outside counsel
**Date:** October 25, 2026
**Re:** Enforceability of §8 (24-month nationwide non-compete) against Wei-Lin Zhao; whether to file in Travis County
**Privileged & confidential — attorney work product**

---

## 1. Question Presented

May Meridian enforce §8 of Zhao's employment agreement — a 24-month, nationwide bar on working for any business that designs or sells warehouse-logistics autonomous mobile robots — against a software engineer who resided and worked full-time in California, signed the form agreement by DocuSign two hours after receiving it without counsel, and is now employed in California by a competitor; and should Meridian file suit in Travis County, Texas, given that §14 chooses Texas law and a Travis County forum?

## 2. Brief Answer

**No on both counts. Do not file in Travis County, and do not send a demand letter threatening §8.**

- **Probability that California law governs the §8 question: ~85–90%.** Two independent routes get Zhao there: Cal. Lab. Code §925 (which, at his election, voids *both* halves of §14 and statutorily assigns California law and a California forum), and the Restatement §187 analysis that Texas and California courts both apply (under which California's §16600 policy is "fundamental" and California has the materially greater interest).
- **Probability Meridian obtains *any* §8 relief from any court: ~3% (range 1%–9%).**

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Which law applies, and why

**Both states use the same test, so the clause is analyzed identically whichever court sits.** Texas applied Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187 in *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990) (`library/desantis_v_wackenhut.md`); California follows §187 in *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992) (`library/nedlloyd_v_superior_court.md`). Under §187(2) the chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties/transaction, **or** (b) application of the chosen law would be contrary to a **fundamental policy** of a state with a **materially greater interest** that would supply the law absent the clause (`library/restatement_187.md`).

- **Prong (a) probably does not help Zhao.** Texas has a substantial relationship: Meridian's HQ, the offer issued by Austin HR, the chosen law, the chosen forum. Assume this prong fails.
- **Prong (b) is where Meridian loses.** California's policy against employee non-competes is expressly "fundamental" (`library/application_group_v_hunter.md`), and it has been codified and *hardened* since 1998: §16600(b)(1) now directs broad reading in line with *Edwards* and voids non-competes "no matter how narrowly tailored" (`library/cal_bpc_16600.md`), while §16600.5(a)–(b) makes the voidness apply "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" and forbids attempts to enforce "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California" (`library/cal_bpc_16600_5.md`). Those two clauses are the California Legislature's own assertion of a materially greater interest, aimed at exactly Meridian's fact pattern.
- **The mirror image of *DeSantis* is the problem.** In *DeSantis* the Texas Supreme Court **refused to honor a Florida choice-of-law clause** in a non-compete because the state where the employee worked (Texas) had the materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy. A California court applying *Nedlloyd* + *Application Group* will run that same machine in reverse and land on §16600. A Texas court applying *DeSantis* is being asked to distinguish its own precedent — it can do so (Zhao worked in California, not Texas; in *Application Group* the employee had been recruited to work **for a California employer**), but it must first explain why the materially-greater-interest state is Texas when the employee lived, worked, and will compete in California for the entire two years.
- **§188 contacts are split, but the center of gravity is California:** residence and place of performance (24 of 24 months) = CA; place of contracting = mixed (offer issued from Austin; executed electronically in CA); employer domicile = TX; locus of the alleged competitive injury = CA; the restraint's entire geographic target includes CA.
- **The decisive point is that §187 is not the only route.** Cal. Lab. Code §925(b) makes §14 **voidable by Zhao**, and once voided at his request, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and **California law shall govern the dispute**" (`library/cal_lab_925.md`). That is a statutory assignment of law and forum that does not depend on winning the §187 argument. See §4.3.

**Conclusion:** California law governs the §8 question in ~85–90% of realistic outcomes. Any litigation plan should be built on that assumption, not on the choice-of-law clause.

### 4.2 Enforceability under each law

**Under California law (most likely applicable): §8 is void.**

- §16600(a) voids every contract restraining "a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind," and (b)(1) requires it be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards*," voiding any employment non-compete "no matter how narrowly tailored" that does not satisfy a statutory exception (`library/cal_bpc_16600.md`).
- *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008) (`library/edwards_v_arthur_andersen.md`) forecloses the intuitive argument that a field-specific carve-out is a "narrow restraint": "Noncompetition agreements are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions." *Edwards* expressly disapproved *Campbell v. Board of Trustees*, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987) and *General Commercial Packaging*, 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997) — both of which are in this library flagged **superseded** and must not be argued (`library/campbell_v_stanford_1987.md`, `library/general_commercial_packaging_1997.md`).
- *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020) closes the other door: the rule of reason applies to **business-to-business** restraints; the employment context is governed by *Edwards* and non-competes are void (`library/ixchel_v_biogen.md`). §8 is squarely an employment restraint.
- **Residual uncertainty, flagged:** §16600 voids restraints "[e]xcept as provided in this chapter," and the chapter's exceptions (sale of business/dissolution-type carve-outs) are **not in this library**. Nothing in our facts suggests one applies (Zhao sold no interest), so this is a formality, not a route. I also cannot state with library support whether §9 (12-month non-solicit) is void; *Edwards*'s library summary addresses non-competition agreements, and §16600(b)(1) speaks to noncompete clauses. Treat §9 as at material risk but unresolved, and note that if it functions as a de facto restraint on taking the Kestrel role it invites the same §16600.5 exposure.

**Under Texas law (the fallback Meridian is hoping for): §8 clears the threshold and then probably fails on scope — and the statutory remedy is reformation with no pre-reformation damages.**

- **Ancillary element — probably satisfied.** §§15.50(a) requires the covenant be "ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made" (`library/tex_bcc_15_50.md`). *Light v. Centel Cellular*, 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994) set the two-part test but its **timing** requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (`library/light_v_centel_1994.md`, status: **modified** — and the library expressly warns it "should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant"). *Sheshunoff Management Services v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006) holds the covenant is enforceable where the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at contracting, and redirects the "core inquiry" to §15.50 reasonableness (`library/sheshunoff_v_johnson.md`). *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011) rejected a narrow "give rise" requirement and accepted consideration reasonably related to protecting goodwill (`library/marsh_usa_v_cook.md`). So §10's confidentiality/invention promises, performed, likely get §8 past the ancillary gate. **This is Meridian's best Texas point and it only gets to the second question.**
- **Reasonableness — the likely failure.** §15.50(a) requires limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** that are reasonable and impose "no greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the promisee's goodwill. §8 is 24 months × the entire United States × the entire field of warehouse-logistics AMRs, for one perception engineer, with no carve-out for non-competing work. Under §15.51(b), **Meridian bears the burden** because the agreement's primary purpose is personal services. A restraint covering an entire industry nationwide, entered on a form with no negotiated confidentiality-specific consideration tied to Zhao, is on its face broader than "necessary."
  - *Flagged as unverified:* **this library contains no Texas case assessing a 24-month, nationwide, industry-wide restraint.** My conclusion that the scope is unreasonable is an inference from the text of §15.50(a), not a cited holding. Do not let it be presented in a brief as case-supported on this library.
- **Remedy ceiling even if Meridian wins:** §15.51(c) — the court **shall reform** an over-broad covenant and enforce it as reformed, **but may not award damages for breach before reformation**. So the Oct. 13 start at Kestrel generates **no damages** in the branch where Meridian "wins" by reformation. §15.52 makes §§15.50–15.51 procedures and remedies **exclusive and preemptive** of other criteria, which also forecloses laundering the claim as a common-law restraint-of-trade or choice-of-law-breach theory.
- §8's clock: termination 2026-09-30 → 24 months runs to **2028-09-30**; a reformed 12-month covenant would end **2027-09-30**, and 25 days (≈3.4% of the period) have already run. Texas courts cannot give the time back.

### 4.4 §16600.5 exposure — suing creates the liability

`library/cal_bpc_16600_5.md`:

- **(c)** "An employer shall **not enter into** a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter." Meridian did that in March 2024 — **already complete, before any lawsuit.**
- **(b)** An employer "shall **not attempt to enforce**" a void contract, regardless of where signed or where employment was maintained. Filing in Travis County *is* the attempt. So is a demand letter that threatens §8 (reading; the library does not define "attempt").
- **(d)** Entering into **or** attempting to enforce a void contract "commits a **civil violation**."
- **(e)(1)** Zhao may bring a **private action** for injunctive relief and/or actual damages. **(e)(2)** a prevailing employee "**shall** be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs" — **mandatory**, not discretionary.

Two features make this asymmetric. First, **the clock runs against Meridian from the filing date**: it cannot settle out of the exposure by declining to win; declining to *file* is the only thing that caps it. Second, **continuing** to prosecute after §925 voids §14 is itself an ongoing "attempt to enforce."

**Company-wide.** §8 is the **standard form for all engineers**. Every California-resident engineer hired on that form since §16600.5 took effect on 1/1/2024 has the same (c) claim, and — if they were current employees on 2024-02-14 — the same notice claim. Zhao is one instance of a program defect, and a public lawsuit is the most likely way the rest of the population learns about it. **Quantifying this requires headcount data we do not have** (Open Item 1).

*Flagged:* whether Zhao's §16600.5(e)(1) "actual damages" are anything beyond nominal for an employee who simply kept working are unknowable here; the **fee award**, not damages, is the driver. ## 5. The strongest argument for each side

**Meridian's best case.** (1) §187(2)(a) is satisfied and prong (b) is not: this is not *Application Group*, where the employee had been recruited to work **for a California employer in California**; Zhao contracted with a Texas employer whose goodwill, HQ, and competitive stake sit in Austin, and §188's place of contracting points to Texas. *DeSantis* protects the policy of the state with the greater interest — and a Texas court is entitled to ask whether California's interest is materially greater than Texas's merely because the employee chose where to live. (2) *Application Group* predates SB 699, and §16600.5's extraterritorial reach is contested (*Westbrook*, per the firm's own file, under en banc review) — so the statute doing the work is not settled law. (3) On the merits, *Sheshunoff* and *Marsh USA* clear the ancillary gate, §15.51(c) makes **reformation** the statutory answer rather than invalidation, and no Texas statute caps 24 months or nationwide geography. (4) §15 recites an opportunity to consult counsel. (5) *Advanced Bionics* means California should not enjoin the Texas suit.

*Why it still loses:* points 1 and 2 are unverifiable in this library; point 3 gets to the merits only to reach a reasonableness problem under §15.50(a) on a burden Meridian carries (§15.51(b)), with damages foreclosed pre-reformation; point 4 is contradicted by Meridian's own HR note, so it evidences the §925(e) problem instead of curing it; and point 5 buys forum, not outcome.

**Zhao's best case.** (1) §925(a)–(b) is a statutory kill shot on §14 built out of Meridian's own documents — offer letter ("fully remote from California"), HR file ("standard form," "no negotiation," "no counsel involved"), executed 2024 — and §925(e) is unavailable because he was not **in fact** individually represented in negotiating §14. Void §14 and California law and a California forum follow by statute, with a discretionary fee award under §925(c). (2) §16600(a) + (b)(1) + *Edwards* void §8 "no matter how narrowly tailored"; *Ixchel* bars the rule-of-reason recharacterization; *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* are dead. (3) §16600.5(a)–(b) removes "you signed it in Texas / employment was in Texas" from the argument. (4) §16600.5(b)+(d) convert Meridian's own lawsuit into a civil violation with **mandatory** fees. (5) §16600.1(a) makes including §8 unlawful *per se*, actionable as unfair competition.

# QUESTIONS FOR THE CLIENT — Meridian / Zhao (§8 non-compete)

Answering these will not change the bottom line (do not file; do not assert §8), but each one moves a number in the exposure model or closes a gap I had to label as an assumption. Where I had to assume, I said so in `memo.md` §8.

## A. Facts I assumed about Zhao

1. **Did Zhao actually start at Kestrel Autonomy on or about 2026-10-13**, and is Kestrel in fact engaged in the design or sale of autonomous mobile robots for warehouse logistics? *(If he has not started, §8's operative period is still unused and the remediation calculus changes; if he started, the delay argument against emergency relief is already baked in.)*
2. **Has any demand letter, cease-and-desist, stop-work letter, or email to Kestrel been sent** — by HR, a manager, or the firm — that mentions §8, §9, or "the non-compete"? If yes: date, sender, exact wording, and whether Kestrel or Zhao forwarded it to counsel. *(Under §16600.5(b) an "attempt to enforce" can be the violation itself; a letter already in the world means the exposure clock may already be running. This is the single most urgent answer.)*
3. **Was Zhao ever a Meridian employee (or contractor) before 2024-02-14**, under any earlier agreement that §8 was added to by amendment or extension? *(This decides whether he was a "current employee" for the §16600.1(b) notice duty, and whether §14 was "modified, or extended" on or after 1/1/2017 under §925(f) — different analysis in both cases.)*
4. **Is there any evidence Zhao removed data, code, models, or documents** — DLP alerts, access logs, device-return audit, USB/cloud egress? *(§10 confidentiality and any trade-secret theory is the only legitimate litigation asset here. Note that trade-secret law is not in my reference library, so a claim would need separate research before filing.)*
5. **What specifically does Meridian believe it loses** if Zhao works at Kestrel — named customers, a roadmap, a cost model? Anything beyond "he is a good engineer at a competitor" is not a legally cognizable injury in California.

## B. The form and the population (drives the real number)

6. **How many California-resident engineers are on, or were hired onto, the standard form containing §8?** Break it out by hire date relative to **2024-02-14** (the §16600.1(b) notice deadline) and **2024-01-01** (the §16600.5 effective date and the "employed after" cut-off), and say how many have already left. *(My pattern-exposure table is linear in this headcount and currently illustrative only.)*
7. **Is the §8 form still being used today** for California-resident hires, and for how long after 2024-01-01 was it used? *(Each California hire on the form is a fresh §16600.5(c) violation; if it is still in use, that is the first thing to stop.)*
8. **Has any notice under §16600.1(b) been sent to anyone** — to Zhao, to other California engineers, or to a subset? Please give the LO-233 ticket text, its owner, and who decided to deprioritize it. *(The deprioritization record is the worst exhibit in the file and determines whether the notice exposure is a compliance gap or a documented knowing omission.)*
9. **Do any other Meridian employees (any state) have §8 variants**, and does any of them have a *negotiated*, counsel-reviewed agreement? *(Determines whether this is a form defect across the board or whether some contracts are defensible.)*

## C. The agreement as a whole (I only have an excerpt)

10. **Is there a prevailing-party attorney's-fee clause anywhere in the full agreement?** Also please provide §§11–13 and 16–18 and any arbitration, class-waiver, PIIA, or severability provisions. *(My model assumes Meridian has NO contractual fee recovery while Zhao has two statutory fee bases. If there is a mutual fee clause, the asymmetry shrinks; if there is an arbitration clause, the whole forum analysis changes.)*
11. **Does the agreement (or a separate PIIA/offer letter) contain a merger or "entire agreement" clause**, and does anything else in the offer package address California law, remote-work terms, or choice of law?
12. **What specific confidential information did Meridian promise or actually give Zhao** under §10 (designs, source, training data, customer lists), and is that documented? *(This is what carries the "ancillary" element under Sheshunoff/Marsh in the Texas-law branch.)*

## D. Prior matters and the firm's own memos

13. **What is the status of the "Alvarez matter"** in which the 2024 memo recommended suing in Travis County? Was suit filed, in what court, on what form of agreement, and is the employee California-based? Was *Calderon* or *Westbrook* cited in a brief? *(If Meridian already sued on this form, the §16600.5 analysis may be live on an existing docket, and the fee exposure may already exist.)*
14. **Is the Zhao file materially different from Alvarez** in any way other than the 2024 execution date?
15. **Can you pull the current status of *Westbrook Systems, Inc. v. Ng* en banc and *Calderon v. Pacific Dynamics*?** Neither is in my library, and the 2025 memo records *Westbrook* as granted rehearing en banc (argued Jan. 2025) with no disposition in our file. Whoever has subscription access needs to confirm whether the extraterritoriality holding survived. *(This is the only authority in the firm's file that would help us, and it is currently unverifiable.)*

## E. Decisions I need from you

16. **Authorize an immediate form change**: drop §8/§9 for California-resident hires going forward. *(Every week of continued use adds violations.)*
17. **Authorize voluntary §16600.1(b)-style notices** (individualized writing, mailing **and** email) to current California employees and qualifying former employees whose contracts contain §8 — or tell me you want that decision escalated. *(Cheap mitigation, versus memorializing that §8 is void in California. My recommendation is to send them.)*
18. **Confirm a litigation hold** on LO-233, the DocuSign metadata, the form-template history, and the §15 recital's drafting history.
19. **Budget/objective check**: if your real goal is deterrence (slowing the next three departures) rather than recovering against Zhao, tell me — the answer is still "don't file," but I would write a different memo about §10 discipline, notice periods, and what to put in future Texas-based hires' agreements.
20. **Confirm no confidential information is at risk** or, if it is, that you want a separate trade-secrets assessment (outside the scope of this library).

cd /work/workspace && python3 - <<'EOF'
import json,os,re
c=json.load(open('deliverable/citations.json'))
idx=open('library/INDEX.md').read()
idxfiles=set(re.findall(r'`([a-zA-Z0-9_/]+\.md)`',idx))
print("entries:",len(c))
bad=[]
for e in c:
    f=e['library_file']
    ok1=f in idxfiles
    ok2=os.path.exists('library/'+f)
    ok3=all(k in e for k in ('cite','library_file','proposition','status_checked'))
    ok4=e['status_checked'] in ('in force','superseded','vacated')
    if not (ok1 and ok2 and ok3 and ok4): bad.append((f,ok1,ok2,ok3,ok4))
    print(f"{'OK ' if ok1 and ok2 else 'BAD'} {f:<45} {e['status_checked']}")
print("problems:",bad)
# check every library file NOT cited is accounted for
cited={e['library_file'] for e in c}
print("\nNot cited:",sorted(idxfiles-cited-{'INDEX.md'}))
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Final, fully-partitioned decision model for Zhao / Meridian sec.8.
Every branch listed exhaustively within each governing-law state; all rows sum.

P_CA   = 0.875   # P(California law governs)          range 0.70 - 0.98
P_TX   = 1 - P_CA

# --- conditional branches if CALIFORNIA law governs (sum to 1.0) ---
CA_VOID = 0.900   # void under 16600 / unenforceable per Edwards-AMN  (sum of 0.88 + 0.02)
CA_ENF  = 0.100   # enforced at all
CA_REAS = 0.100   # 24-month nationwide held reasonable | enforced
CA_STOP = 0.500   # order actually ends the Kestrel job | enforced + reasonable
CA_INT  = 0.200   # interlocutory relief | enforced + unreasonable (then loses at final)

# --- conditional branches if TEXAS law governs (sum to 1.0) ---
TX_VOID = 0.877   # unenforceable: overbroad, covenants-not-to-abuse-nothing doctrine
TX_ENF  = 0.123
TX_REAS = 0.300
TX_STOP = 0.500
TX_INT  = 0.200

def outcome(p_law, p_void, p_enf, p_reas, p_stop, p_int):
    """Return dict of absolute probabilities summing to p_law."""
    o = {}
    o["unenforceable"] = p_law * p_void
    enf_reas  = p_law * p_enf * p_reas
    enf_unre  = p_law * p_enf * (1 - p_reas)
    o["wins_all"]    = enf_reas * p_stop              # final injunction, job ends
    o["reasonable_but_nothing"] = enf_reas * (1 - p_stop)  # order that doesn't stop the job
    o["reformed_interim"] = enf_unre * p_int          # delay only, loses at final
    o["reformed_nothing"] = enf_unre * (1 - p_int)
    return o

tx = outcome(P_TX, TX_VOID, TX_ENF, TX_REAS, TX_STOP, TX_INT)
tot = {k: ca.get(k, 0) + tx.get(k, 0) for k in set(ca) | set(tx)}
assert abs(sum(tot.values()) - 1.0) < 1e-9

def pct(x): return f"{100*x:6.2f}%"

print("=== OUTCOMES, absolute (sum to 100%) ===")
for k in ["unenforceable", "reformed_nothing", "reformed_interim", "reasonable_but_nothing", "wins_all"]:
    print(f"  {k:28s} {pct(tot[k])}")
print(f"  CHECK total                  {pct(sum(tot.values()))}")

any_relief   = tot["wins_all"] + tot["reasonable_but_nothing"] + tot["reformed_interim"]
stop_the_job = tot["wins_all"]
print(f"\nP(some court order of any kind)  {pct(any_relief)}")

base, equity, misc = 182_000, 30_000, 12_000

def neg(x): return -x

    # expected $ for the branch, $k
    val = (1 - relief_prob - win_prob) * neg(no_relief_fees + liab_amt + opp)
    val += relief_prob * neg(fees_interim + liab_amt + opp_interim)
    val += win_prob    * (1_766_000 - fees_win - opp_win)

print(f"  wins everything: value 1766 - fees 150 - opp 8 = {(0.01*15_000_000-182_000-30_000) - (150_000+8_000):,}")

    return None

iCA = CA_ENF*(1-CA_REAS)*CA_INT
print("\n=== EXPECTED VALUE ($k) ===")
print(f"  branches if CA law:   no relief {1-rCA-iCA:.3f}   interim/partial {iCA:.3f}   reasonable {rCA:.3f}")
print(f"  no-relief cost {NO_RELIEF_COST:,}   interim cost {INTERIM_COST:,}")
ev_base = overall_ev(P_CA, rCA, iCA, NO_RELIEF_COST, INTERIM_COST)
print(f"  EV(filing) base  = {ev_base:,.0f}k")

print("pCA  rCA   iCA   P(any)  P(stop)  P(liab)  EV$k")
rows=[]
for p_ca in (0.70, 0.80, 0.875, 0.95, 0.98):
    for rCA_s in (0.005, 0.01, 0.02):

for label, no_c, in_c in [("low  (fees 120k, no Zhao-fee award)",  120_000+12_000+8_000,  150_000+12_000),

    print(f"  {label:42s} EV {overall_ev(P_CA, rCA, iCA, no_c, in_c):8.0f}k")

"""Final decision model, Meridian v. Zhao sec.8. Exhaustive partitions; all rows sum."""

P_CA, CA_STOP, CA_INT, TX_STOP, TX_INT = 0.875, 0.50, 0.20, 0.50, 0.20

def outcomes(p_law, p_void, p_enf, p_reas):
    o = {"unenforceable": p_law * p_void}
    er, eu = p_law * p_enf * p_reas, p_law * p_enf * (1 - p_reas)
    o["wins_all"]                = er * p_stop          # injunction that actually ends the Kestrel job
    o["reasonable_but_nothing"]  = er * (1 - p_stop)    # order on the books, job continues
    o["reformed_interim"]        = eu * p_int           # TRO-then-loses: delay only
    o["reformed_nothing"]        = eu * (1 - p_int)
    return o

def model(p_ca=0.875, ca_enf=0.10, ca_reas=0.10, tx_enf=0.123, tx_reas=0.30):
    ca = outcomes(p_ca,   1-ca_enf, ca_enf, ca_reas)
    tx = outcomes(1-p_ca, 1-tx_enf, tx_enf, tx_reas)
    tot = {k: ca[k] + tx[k] for k in ca}
    return p_ca, ca, tx, tot

p_ca, ca, tx, tot = model()
keys = ["unenforceable", "reformed_nothing", "reformed_interim", "reasonable_but_nothing", "wins_all"]

def any_relief(o):  return o["wins_all"] + o["reasonable_but_nothing"] + o["reformed_interim"]

print("=== ABSOLUTE OUTCOMES (sum 100%) ===")
for k in keys: print(f"  {k:26s} {100*tot[k]:6.2f}%")
print(f"  {'TOTAL':26s} {100*sum(tot.values()):6.2f}%")
print(f"P(any court order)      {100*any_relief(tot):5.1f}%")
print(f"P(order ends Kestrel job) {100*tot['wins_all']:5.1f}%")

print("\n=== CONDITIONAL ON CALIFORNIA LAW (sum 100%) ===")
for k in keys: print(f"  {k:26s} {100*ca[k]/p_ca:6.2f}%")
print(f"  P(any order | CA)       {100*any_relief(ca)/p_ca:6.2f}%   P(ends job | CA) {100*ca['wins_all']/p_ca:.2f}%")

print("\n=== CONDITIONAL ON TEXAS LAW (sum 100%) ===")
for k in keys: print(f"  {k:26s} {100*tx[k]/(1-p_ca):6.2f}%")
print(f"  P(any order | TX)       {100*any_relief(tx)/(1-p_ca):6.2f}%   P(ends job | TX) {100*tx['wins_all']/(1-p_ca):.2f}%")

ca_any_c = any_relief(ca) / p_ca           # 0.028
liab = p_ca * (1 - ca_any_c)
print(f"\nP(affirmative 16600.5 exposure by filing) = 0.875 x (1 - {ca_any_c:.3f}) = {100*liab:.1f}%")
print(f"P(judgment for Meridian on the merits, any theory) = {100*(tot['wins_all']+tot['reasonable_but_nothing']):.2f}%")

# ---------- money ----------
# memo 7.3 stack, $k:  own fees 220 | Zhao's fee award 240 | 16600.5 exposure 30 | misc 12 | opportunity 30
NO_RELIEF = 220 + 240 + 30 + 12 + 30          # 542  (memo 7.3 'no relief' row, fees+costs; lost profits separate)
# but 16600.5 exposure attaches in EVERY CA-law loss, incl. interim-only.  memo used 634 = 542 + 92? fix: build
# the stack exactly once and use it everywhere.

COST_INTERIM   = 350 + 240 + 30 + 12 + 20     # longer fight, ends in settlement: = 652
WIN_VALUE      = 0.01*15_000_000 - 182 - 30 - 150 - 8   # 1% x 15M less comp/fees/opp, $k  (illustrative)
print(f"\nWIN-EVERYTHING VALUE check: 150 - 182 - 30 - 150 - 8 = {WIN_VALUE:,.0f}k  (negative even on a total win)")

def ev(ca_enf=0.10, ca_reas=0.10, p_ca=0.875, no_c=COST_NO_RELIEF, in_c=COST_INTERIM):
    _, ca_, tx_, tot_ = model(p_ca, ca_enf, ca_reas)
    ca_nr  = 1 - any_relief(ca_)/p_ca
    ca_in  = (any_relief(ca_) - ca_["wins_all"])/p_ca
    ca_w   = ca_["wins_all"]/p_ca
    ca_ev  = ca_nr*(-no_c) + ca_in*(-in_c) + ca_w*(WIN_VALUE if WIN_VALUE > 0 else -in_c)
    tx_nr  = 1 - any_relief(tx_)/(1-p_ca)
    tx_in  = any_relief(tx_)/(1-p_ca)          # TX branch: any order treated as interim
    tx_ev  = tx_nr*(-no_c) + tx_in*(-in_c)
    return p_ca*ca_ev + (1-p_ca)*tx_ev

            _, ca_, _, tot_ = model(pca, enf, reas)
            row = (pca, enf, reas,
                   100*any_relief(tot_), 100*tot_["wins_all"],
                   100*pca*(1-any_relief(ca_)/pca), ev(enf, reas, pca))
            grid.append(row)
            print(f" {row[0]:.3f} {row[1]:.2f}  {row[2]:.2f}   {row[3]:5.1f}    {row[4]:5.2f}    {row[5]:5.1f}  {row[6]:7.0f}")
print("grid min/max: P(any) %.1f-%.1f%%  P(stop) %.2f-%.2f%%  P(liab) %.0f-%.0f%%  EV %.0fk..%.0fk" % (
    min(r[3] for r in grid), max(r[3] for r in grid),
    min(r[4] for r in grid), max(r[4] for r in grid),
    min(r[5] for r in grid), max(r[5] for r in grid),
    min(r[6] for r in grid), max(r[6] for r in grid)))

print("\ncost-side EV:")
for lab, nc, ic in [("optimistic: fees 120, no Zhao-fee award, expo 0",  120+12+8,          150+12),
                    ("base",                                              COST_NO_RELIEF,     COST_INTERIM),
                    ("pessimistic: 300+400+60+12+30",                     300+400+60+12+30,  400+400+60+12+20)]:
    print(f"  {lab:52s} EV {ev(0.10,0.10,0.875,nc,ic):7.0f}k")

# ---------- sec.8 clock ----------
from datetime import date
t = date(2026, 9, 30)
print(f"\nterminated {t}  |  sec.8 as written ends {date(2028,9,30)}  |  if reformed to 12 mo, {date(2027,9,30)}")
elapsed = (date(2026,10,25) - t).days
print(f"elapsed {(date(2026,10,25)-t).days}d = {100*(date(2026,10,25)-t).days/730:.1f}% of the 24-mo term")

# ---------- pattern exposure ----------
rows=[("2025-Q2",2,2),("2025-Q3",4,3),("2025-Q4",3,3),("2025-Q1",1,1),("2026-Q1",4,2)]
print(f"\npattern: {sum(r[1] for r in rows)} exits / 5 quarters = {sum(r[1] for r in rows)/5:.1f} per quarter"
      f" (HR sheet avg 2.8); competing-role cites {sum(r[2] for r in rows)} of 14 = {100*sum(r[2] for r in rows)/14:.0f}%")
for n,lo,hi in [(25,12_500,20_000),(75,12_500,20_000)]:
    print(f"  {n:3d} claimants x 12.5-20k = {n*lo:,} - {n*hi:,}")
for n in (50,200): print(f"  {n:3d} claimants x 5,000      = {n*5_000:,}")
for n,lo,hi in [(25,2_500,7_500),(75,2_500,7_500),(150,2_500,7_500)]:
    print(f"  {n:3d} claimants x 2.5-7.5k  = {n*lo:,} - {n*hi:,}")

Code §925 (which, at his election, voids *both* halves of §14 and statutorily assigns California law and a California forum), and the Restatement §187 analysis that Texas and California courts both apply (under which California's §16600 policy is "fundamental" and California has the materially greater interest).
memo.md:20:- **Probability Meridian obtains *any* §8 relief from any court: ~3% (range 1%–9%).**
memo.md:21:- **Probability Meridian obtains relief that actually stops the Kestrel Autonomy job: ~1% (range 1%–3%).** Even a Texas injunction would face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds (`library/tx_jurisdiction_note.md`), so the realistic product of suit is an unenforceable order and two forums' worth of fees.
memo.md:23:- **Probability Meridian creates affirmative liability for itself by filing: ~85–90%, essentially one-way.** §16600.5 makes the *attempt to enforce* a void contract a civil violation, and makes a fee award to a prevailing employee mandatory. Meridian's exposure starts the moment it files — before it can lose.
memo.md:24:- **Expected net cost of filing: roughly −$600k** (range −$390k to −$900k, before any company-wide notice/UCL claims). Arithmetic in §7.
memo.md:63:**Conclusion:** California law governs the §8 question in ~85–90% of realistic outcomes. Any litigation plan should be built on that assumption, not on the choice-of-law clause.
memo.md:80:- §8's clock: termination 2026-09-30 → 24 months runs to **2028-09-30**; a reformed 12-month covenant would end **2027-09-30**, and 25 days (≈3.4% of the period) have already run. Texas courts cannot give the time back.
memo.md:163:1. **Do not file in Travis County. Do not assert §8.** Probability of meaningful relief ≈ 1–3%; probability of creating §1660.5 liability by filing ≈ 85–90%; expected net cost ≈ −$600k. Even the "deterrence" rationale is thin: a case this likely to be dismissed on jurisdiction and choice of law does not deter other engineers; a fee award against Meridian that other engineers' counsel read about does the opposite.
